summary: This section explains how certain companies must form special committees to handle director appointments, pay policies, and security holder complaints. It sets rules for who can sit on these committees and requires committee leaders to attend general meetings. If companies break these rules, they face fines.
points: Listed public companies and other prescribed companies must form a Nomination and Remuneration Committee with at least three non-executive directors.
At least half of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee members must be independent directors.
The committee must find qualified people for directorships and senior management, recommend their appointment or removal, and set performance evaluation rules.
The committee must create a pay policy that attracts good talent, links pay to performance, and balances fixed and incentive pay.

Companies with more than one thousand security holders at any time during a financial year must form a Stakeholders Relationship Committee led by a non-executive director to resolve security holder grievances.
Committee chairpersons or their authorised members must attend the company general meetings.
example: Sunrise Retail Limited is a listed public company in India with over one thousand security holders. To follow the law, the board of directors forms a Nomination and Remuneration Committee consisting of three non-executive directors, ensuring that at least half of them are independent. The board also sets up a Stakeholders Relationship Committee led by a non-executive director to address complaints from security holders. One day, a security holder named Rahul submits a grievance about delayed communication. The Stakeholders Relationship Committee reviews the issue in good faith. Meanwhile, the chairperson of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee attends the upcoming general meeting to answer relevant questions from the shareholders.

terms.meaning: A board member who is not involved in the day-to-day management of the company.
A board member who does not have any material or pecuniary relationship with the company.
Top corporate officers like the chief executive officer, managing director, or company secretary.
An act that breaks a law or rule.

watch: Failing to resolve a security holder grievance in good faith does not automatically count as breaking the law.
